statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later, and the one general-population test read here, for alcohol, did not find the full pattern. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among all 38,309 people who had ever drunk, men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink); since the times below were similar, this mostly reflects men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent, not faster progression. Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted) and shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years). Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the 1989 study that named telescoping timed 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups, in whom the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter in women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). Narrative reviews by one research group list faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and prescription opioids, but not heroin, mostly in treatment samples (McHugh et al., 2018, which explains the difference from population surveys by who reaches treatment; Greenfield et al., 2007, which calls it one of the most reproducible findings); a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men is described, without its timing measure or adjustment, as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). Randall et al. (1999), the Project MATCH treatment-sample study, which the papers read describe in opposite ways, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men? This has not been shown for women in general. The idea, called 'telescoping', came from small groups of people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened, and its stages were first drawn from men's stories. In two big US surveys of ordinary adults, women had their first drink later than men and were less likely to become dependent on alcohol. Among the people who did become dependent, women got there about as fast as men, on average about 6 years after their first drink, and a little faster in one age group. A review suggests that the women who reach treatment may have more severe problems, which would explain why faster problems show up in treatment. All these studies relied on memory, and the surveys were only about alcohol. See the contested question.
population: Adults in two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002; US-born, aged 18 to 57; 53,238 people, 38,309 of whom had ever drunk) for alcohol; for other drugs and for treatment and self-help samples, studies described in a historical critique and two narrative reviews
exposure: Being a woman (the studies compare by gender and do not separate sex from gender)
outcome: Time from first use to dependence and from dependence to first treatment ('telescoping'), every step recalled at one interview or in questionnaires
magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers, men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). Treatment and self-help samples, second-hand (Marks & Clark, 2018): founding study, 33 women and 105 men, first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter in women, first drink about 2 and first intoxication about 3 years later in women, same age at treatment entry; Iowa treatment centres (3,132 men, 395 women), treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit in women, about 3 in men; national cannabis sample (1,217 women, 3,297 men), first use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women; 75 of 103 citing articles used the founding study as background.

risk_of_bias.note: Every timing was recalled at a single interview or in questionnaires, years or decades later (card sc_keyes_2010: JBI, moderate); treatment samples select people by having reached treatment and are known here only through reviews that did not appraise them (cards sc_marks_2018, sc_mchugh_2018, sc_greenfield_2007); in the survey analysis the hazards among all drinkers mix the chance of dependence with its speed, the averages among people who became dependent are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, and several table and text values disagree.

inconsistency.note: Treatment samples and the general-population analysis point in different directions, and within the survey paper the hazards (men faster) and the averages among people who became dependent (no difference overall; women faster in one cohort) differ; the review explains this by sample, which is plausible but untested.

indirectness.note: The only general-population test read concerns alcohol, in US-born adults aged 18 to 57 interviewed in 1991–1992 and 2001–2002; the evidence for other drugs and from treatment samples is second-hand (narrative reviews; METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: The survey estimates are precise (at least 4,603 people per cohort); the small treatment samples (33 women in the founding study) are part of the second-hand evidence already rated down.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; that 75 of 103 papers citing the founding study used it without testing it concerns citation, not publication.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. Counted once: McHugh et al. (2018) updates Greenfield et al. (2007) by the same group and reuses its search; both reviews and the critique describe overlapping treatment-sample studies and the same general-population analysis (Keyes et al., 2010), so they add no independent data; the survey analysis pools NLAES, which Greenfield et al. also cite through Dawson (1996). Each figure is labelled with its quantity: hazards among all drinkers (chance and speed together) or averages among people who reached the step (speed only). Randall et al. (1999), the Project MATCH treatment-sample study, is not yet read and is described in opposite ways by the papers read; reading it, and Khan et al. (2013) for cannabis, could change the yes side. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways (treatment samples against the general-population survey), with a published critique of the concept, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Do women go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men, or does the faster course seen in treatment samples come from who reaches treatment and from how the timing was remembered?
debate.evidence_yes: The faster course was described in people in treatment. In the 1989 study that named telescoping, 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups recalled their landmark ages: the women had started drinking about 2 years later and had first been drunk about 3 years later, entered treatment at the same age, and went from their first alcohol-related problem to their first treatment 4.3 years faster on average; in an earlier Iowa treatment sample (3,132 men and 395 women), women reached treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit and men about 3 (as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). Narrative reviews list faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids (McHugh et al., 2018) and call it one of the most reproducible findings (Greenfield et al., 2007). A national cannabis sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men is described as finding the time from first use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, which would be evidence outside treatment if it is a general-population sample (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018; not read here, and cited to a different paper by McHugh et al., 2018). In the general-population surveys, among the people who did become dependent, women born 1964–1973 got there faster than men (on average 3.7 against 4.2 years), the printed figures suggest the same for women born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4 years, not marked significant; an editors' approximation on the study card), and among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010).
debate.evidence_no: In the only general-population test read, two pooled US national surveys (1991–1992 and 2001–2002; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57), women started drinking later than men, but among all lifetime drinkers men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every birth cohort (1.36 to 1.79) and, among people with dependence, a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in two of five cohorts, 1.55 and 1.42), after adjustment for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink; among people who became dependent, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years); the authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population (Keyes et al., 2010). A narrative review explains the gap between treatment samples and population surveys by who is sampled, since women who reach treatment likely have more severe disorders, and reports that telescoping was not found for heroin (McHugh et al., 2018). The historical critique shows that the stages that define telescoping were drawn from the recalled histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed, 15 women's answers set aside), that the founding 1989 study was small and drawn from treatment and self-help settings, and that 75 of 103 papers citing it used it as background without testing it; it argues that, with women as the reference group, men's longer course might have been called magnification, and recommends discarding the term (Marks & Clark, 2018).
debate.neither_can_show: Every timing in these studies was recalled, often decades later, at a single interview or in a questionnaire; none was recorded as it happened, and no study read tested whether women and men remember timing differently (the surveys' recall check tested only whether later-starting dependence was forgotten over 10 years). Treatment samples time only people who reached treatment, so a group that reaches treatment soon after its problems begin will look fast whatever its course in the population. In the general-population surveys, hazards among all drinkers combine the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, so a higher hazard in men mostly says that more men become dependent; the averages among people who became dependent come closer to speed but are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, and the youngest cohort could contribute only steps completed by age 27. People who died before the surveys, or were older than 57, are missing. None of these designs separates sex (biology) from gender (roles, access to treatment, stigma), and the general-population evidence read is for alcohol in the USA only.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The faster course in women was described in small treatment and self-help samples, from recalled ages, and the idea grew out of stage models built from men's recalled histories. In the one general-population test read, for alcohol in the USA, women were less likely than men to become dependent and to reach treatment, and those who did become dependent got there about as fast as men on average, faster in one birth cohort. So the evidence read here does not show that women in general move faster from first use to dependence; whether women who do develop dependence move faster, and whether this holds for other drugs, is open. The studies that bear most directly on the yes side, Randall et al. (1999) for alcohol in a treatment sample and Khan et al. (2013) for cannabis, are known here only from other papers' descriptions, which disagree about the first.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young women and men followed from before first use, with use, dependence criteria and treatment recorded as they happen (repeated interviews or linked records), analysed with methods that separate the chance of ever becoming dependent from the speed of progression among those who do (for example mixture-cure or competing-risks models), with sex (including hormonal status) and gender (roles, access to treatment) measured separately; and a systematic review of telescoping studies, drug by drug, that separates treatment from general-population samples and recalled from prospectively recorded timing.
